3. Data Sources

Observed Data

The graph presents a reconstruction of absolute sea level developed by Australia’s Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organisation (CSIRO). This reconstruction is available through 2013 and is based on two main data sources:

  • Satellite data from the TOPography EXperiment (TOPEX)/Poseidon, Jason-1, and Jason-2 satellite altimeters, operated by the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) and France’s Centre National d’Etudes Spatiales (CNES).
  • Tide gauge measurements compiled by the Permanent Service for Mean Sea Level (PSMSL), which includes more than a century of daily and monthly tide gauge data.

The graph also presents the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s (NOAA’s) analysis of altimeter data from the TOPEX/Poseidon and Jason-1, -2, and -3 satellite missions. These data are available through 2023.

Maps present relative sea level trends calculated by NOAA based on measurements from permanent tide gauge stations. The original data come from the National Water Level Observation Network (NWLON), operated by the Center for Operational Oceanographic Products and Services (CO-OPS) within NOAA’s National Ocean Service (NOS).

Projections

Projections come from NOAA via Sweet et al. (2022). These are the U.S. federal government’s official sea level scenarios, which were developed by an interagency task force to feed into the Fifth National Climate Assessment.

NOAA’s 2022 release includes five scenarios. The project team selected two at the recommendation of NOAA and because they align most closely to the range of emissions scenarios that the team is using for GCM-based pairings:

  • Intermediate-low, which corresponds to 0.5 meters of global mean sea level rise between 2000 and 2100. The project team has labeled this scenario “lower sea level rise” in the graphics to reduce the chance of it being conflated with the “intermediate” emissions scenario. This scenario can result from emissions scenarios ranging from SSP1-1.9 through SSP3-7.0. Given current sea level observations and estimates of future warming, this scenario provides a reasonable estimate of the lower bound for the most likely sea level rise by 2100.
  • Intermediate, which corresponds to 1 meter of global mean sea level rise between 2000 and 2100. The project team has labeled this scenario “higher sea level rise” in the graphics to reduce the chance of it being conflated with the “intermediate” emissions scenario. This scenario can result from emissions scenarios ranging from SSP2-4.5 through SSP5-8.5. This scenario provides a reasonable upper bound for the most likely range of sea level rise by 2100.

NOAA’s other three scenarios include one lower sea level scenario and two appreciably higher trajectories. The higher sea level rise scenarios represent low-confidence but high-impact possibilities—namely, rapid ice melt associated with major “tipping points” reached on Greenland and/or Antarctica.

These scenarios are not truly model outputs, so the project team is referring to them as “projections” or “scenarios,” not “model outputs” as other pairings present.

4. Data Availability

Observed Data

The CSIRO long-term tide gauge reconstruction has been published online in graph form, and the data are posted on CSIRO’s website. CSIRO’s website also provides a list of tide gauges that were used to develop the long-term tide gauge reconstruction.

The satellite time series was obtained from NOAA’s Laboratory for Satellite Altimetry, which maintains an online repository of sea level data (NOAA, 2024). The data file for this indicator was downloaded from this site. Underlying satellite measurements can be obtained from NASA’s online database (NASA, 2022). The reconstructed tide gauge time series is based on data from the PSMSL database.

The relative sea level map and inset plots are based on individual station measurements that can be accessed through NOAA’s “Sea Level Trends” website. This website also presents an interactive map that illustrates sea level trends over different timeframes. NOAA has not published the specific table of 1960–2023 trends that it provided to the project team for this analysis; however, a user could reproduce these numbers from the publicly available data cited above. NOAA periodically publishes a version of this trend analysis that was originally published in a technical report on long-term sea level variations of the United States (NOAA, 2009).

Projections

The sea level projections featured here can be downloaded as part of the companion data files to Sweet et al. (2022).
